title: Do Cu Substrates Participate in Bi Electrocatalytic CO2 Reduction?
abstract: Bi based electrocatalysts for CO2 reduction have recently attracted much research attention. Although Cu substrates were mainly used in these material investigations, whether the Cu substrates act as the CO2 reduction electrocatalysts is questionable, and yet disregarded. Herein to comprehensively investigate the influence of Cu substrate on the electrochemical performance, we electrodeposited Bi catalysts on Cu foams. It was found that during the whole process, the morphology and composition of Bi/ Cu electrocatalysts varied, indicating that Cu acted as not only the electrode substrates but also the active materials for CO2 reduction. After optimization, Bi/Cu materials achieved high activity of 59.7 mAcm 2 and selectivity of 95% for CO2 converted formate. Our work provides experimental evidence for the material design and optimization of Bi-based materials for CO2 reduction. Combustion of fossil fuels has increasingly caused severe greenhouse gas emission, leading to worldwide research interest focusing on electrochemical CO2 fixation. [2] As a potential CO2 immobilization technology, electrocatalytic CO2 reduction has attracted wide attention. Recently, various metallic materials have been applied as CO2 electrocatalytic materials, among which Bi-based materials are widely concerned as a great electrocatalyst for CO2 converting into formate with high efficiency and selectivity. Many studies focused on Bi morphologies-efficiency relationships, in which Cu was used as the substrates during the preparation of Bi catalysts. Some reports believed that the Cu foams provide a highly conductive, and three-dimensional electrode framework for the deposition of Bi. Therefore they improved the CO2 converting efficiencies. However, as an electrocatalytic material for CO2 reduction, [18] whether the Cu substrates act as the CO2 reduction electrocatalysts is questionable, and yet disregarded. To determine the function and evolution process of Cu after Bi depositing on Cu substrates, in this study, we electrodeposited nanocoral-like Bi catalysts on Cu foams. It was shown that a few Cu have dissolved and re-deposited onto Bi electrocatalysts. After long-term CO2 conversion, the proportion of Bi and Cu was gradually stabilized in the composite material on the surface of Cu foam. Meanwhile, the morphology of catalysts changed to nanoneedle-like, indicating the transfer of Cu from the catalyst surface to the framework. Through optimization, Bi/ Cu materials achieve high activity and selectivity of CO2 conversion to formate. Our work provides experimental evidence for the material design and optimization of Bi based materials for CO2 reduction. Similar to previous literature, Bi-based catalysts were prepared by electrodeposition onto Cu foam. The characteristics of the prepared Bi/Cu catalyst electrodes were shown in figure 1. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (figure 1a) images showed that the Cu foam was coated by nano-coral-like structures. This morphological feature can be confirmed by transmission electron microscopy (TEM) (figure 1b). High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) showed the lattice d-spacing with an average size of 0.329 nm, corresponding to the (012) face lattice distance of metallic Bi, indicating the coral-like microstructure is composed of Bi. Moreover, the elemental distribution results by energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscope (EDS) elemental analysis were presented in figure 1c–e. Interestingly, the images revealed that both Bi and Cu were distributed uniformly on the coral-like structure, indicating that the co-deposition of Bi and Cu has taken place during the deposition process. Figure 1f shows the X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of the as-prepared catalyst. It is obvious that most of the diffraction peaks of the catalysts correspond to a typical rhombohedral metallic Bi (PDF#85-1331) with the highest peak intensity at 27.26° corresponds to the (012) face of Bi. Nevertheless, an obscure Cu reflection can be observed in the diffractogram at 50.3°, indexing to (200) plane of cubic Cu (PDF#70-3038), suggesting that the electrocatalyst is a Bi/Cu composite with Bi as the matrix. The surface chemical features of the freshprepared Bi/Cu electrocatalysts was elucidated via X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS). Figure 1g presents the XPS Bi 4 f analysis, the Bi4f7/2 and Bi4f5/2 signals can be ascribed with metallic Bi at 156.7 eV and 162.1 eV, and the shoulder peaks at 158.9 eV and 164.2 eV are related to Bi3+, respectively.[6] The Cu2p3/2 XPS spectra at 932.2 eV and 933.8 eV in figure 1h indicate the state of metallic Cu and Cu2+ which may be caused by surficial oxidation during the preparation of the catalyst.[23]
Then the Bi/Cu electrode was pretreated by cyclic voltammetry for 50 cycles in CO2-saturated 0.5 M KHCO3 solutions. Figure 2 displays the microscopic morphology and structure of the pretreated Bi catalysts. From the SEM image of Bi/Cu catalysts (Figure 2a), It can be observed that the coral structure changed into thin flakes with an average nanosheet size at 0.90 μm after pretreatment. For more detailed morphology, TEM and EDS element mapping images in Figure 2b-d showed that Bi and Cu were uniformly distributed. Figure 2e depicts the XRD pattern of the catalyst. The characteristic diffraction peaks corresponding to Bi (PDF# 85–1331). Sharp peaks at 43.2°, 50.3°, and 73.9° were observed on pretreated catalysts, corresponding to Cu (PDF#70-3038), indicating Cu crystallization. Figure 2f shows the Bi 4 f XPS spectra. Two different peaks at 156.6 eV and 162.0 eV should be assigned to Bi 4f7/2 and Bi 4f5/2, respectively. The Bi 4 f signals at 158.8 eV and 164.1 eV fit to Bi3+, respectively. The increase of Bi3+ content compared with that before pretreatment is due to the oxidation of some Bi during surface activation.[24] As for the Cu 2p XPS spectrum, new peaks at 933.1 and 952.6 eV can be assigned to Cu+. The characteristics of the deposited catalysts after cyclic voltammetry revealed the evolution of Bi/Cu composite with different structures and valence on the Cu foam substrate.

After pretreatment, a long-term stability test over 10 hours was carried out with the Bi/Cu electrodes. As the morphological characteristics shown in figure 3a-d, the flake structure after pretreatment replaced to needle structures. These changes should be induced by the structural reorganization of Bi/Cu during the process of CO2 reduction. XRD patterns confirm Bi2O2CO3 (PDF#84-1752) and Cu2O (PDF#78-2076) phases after stability tests with the peaks of Cu substrates (figure 3e), indicating that Bi adsorbed CO3
2 and converted into Bi2O2CO3 after a long time reaction in the KHCO3 solution. Under the condition of CO2 reduction, Cu existed in the form of Cu
+. Further evidence of the evolution from Bi to Bi2O2CO3 could be found by the XPS spectrum (figure 3f), the peaks at approximately 158.7 eV and 164.1 eV correspond to Bi3+.[25] And for Cu 2p, in addition to the Cu peak exposed on the Cu substrate, the existence of Cu+ at 932.47 eV and 952.5 eV confirmed the results of XRD.[26,27]
The above results show that the substrate Cu were gradually incorporated into the Bi catalyst and participate in the CO2 reduction process. However, the effect on the performance of the catalysts was not clear. At the same time, although we have a preliminary understanding of the morphology and composition changes of Bi/Cu, the mechanism of the evolution process is unknown. Therefore, we first carried out the performance test of CO2 reduction for Bi/Cu catalysts.
The electrocatalytic reduction of CO2 performance was evaluated in 0.5 M CO2 saturated KHCO3 solution in a typical Htype electrochemical cell. To study the performance of the electrode, the products during the CO2 reduction process on Bi/ Cu electrodes were quantitatively analyzed by applying within the voltage range of 0.7~-1.2 VRHE on Cu foam. The Faradaic efficiencies of the products respect to potentials are shown in figure 4a. For the primary product, the Faradaic efficiency of formate (FEformate) generation increased to 95% at 0.9 VRHE, and kept close to 100% in a potential window between 0.9 and 1.2 VRHE. Furthermore, only a small amount of CO (FECO<2%)

The formate partial current density (Jformate) increased from 4.76 to 59.68 mA/cm2 from 0.7 to 1.2 VRHE, suggesting the high catalytic activity of Bi/Cu catalysts. The stability of the Bi electrodes for electrochemical CO2 reduction was investigated through a long term operation at 0.9 VRHE for 13 h (figure 4b). The current density keeps comparably stable at approximately 26.17 mA/cm2. Furthermore, the FEformate maintained over 80% for approximately 10 hours, indicating the prominent stability of the Bi/Cu catalysts.
To determine the function of Cu involved in CO2 reduction, the Bix-Cuy catalysts were fabricated on carbon paper, where x and y represent the stoichiometric ratios of BiCl3 and CuCl2 solution during the fabrication process. Faraday efficiency and partial density of formate were plotted as a function of the stoichiometric ratio (figure 4c). From the Bi1-Cu0 to Bi1-Cu1 electrodes, the FEformate increased gradually and the partial current density maintained a similar tendency. The FEformate of Bi4-Cu1 and Bi1-Cu1 electrodes remained above ~95%, similar to the experimental data, implying Cu was involved in the CO2 reduction reaction. The highest FEformate occurred around 1 :1, the FEformate was around 99.8% and the current density was
7.5 mAcm 2. After that, with the increase of the amount of Cu, the FEformate and Jformate decreased sharply to 21.8% and 1.2 mAcm 2 of the Bi0-Cu1 electrodes. The results show that the presence of suitable Cu can also make the catalyst have high CO2 catalytic activity and selectivity.
Besides, the as-prepared Bi1-Cu0, Bi1-Cu1, and Bi0-Cu1 electrodes on carbon capper were also characterized by SEM, and the results are as shown in figure 4d-e. The transformation of morphology is obvious. Firstly, the pristine Bi sample shows typical nanosheets structures of Bi. As a mixture of Bi and Cu, the Bi1-Cu1 shows coral-like morphology. And pristine Cu shows an acicular morphology. The insert diagram lists the surface Bi/ Cu ratios of catalysts for as-prepared, pretreated, and long-term applied Bi/Cu catalysts. Obviously, the ratio on the surface increased.

In this paper, we firstly confirmed that Cu substrates participated in the CO2 reduction reaction when Cu was used as the substrates, and the performance of the catalytic reaction was affected by the change of morphology and ratio. The evolution of Bi/Cu morphology is accompanied by the whole CO2 reduction process, and the ratio of Bi and Cu plays an important role of electrochemical CO2 convert to HCOOH. Bi/Cu catalyst transformed from nano-coral, nano-flake, to nanoneedle like composite in the whole process. Based on the synergistic reaction, it is found that the Bi/Cu shows a maximum FEformate of 95% and a Jformate of 59.7 mA/cm
2. This work will be helpful for the material design and optimization of Bi based materials for CO2 reduction.
